name: Heinrich Rohrer
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Rohrer was still a PhD student at ETH Zurich at age 26; his doctorate was completed in February 1960 at age 27. The scanning tunneling microscope invention (1981) and Nobel Prize (1986) came decades later.
early_history_summary: Rohrer grew up in Buchs, Switzerland, and moved to Zurich in 1949. He studied physics at ETH Zurich from 1951 to 1955, then began his PhD on superconductivity under Jörgen Lykke Olsen, completing it in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born in Buchs, St. Gallen, Switzerland as the third child; family moved to Zurich in 1949. Enjoyed a carefree childhood with freedom, school, and farm work.
evidence_summary: Rohrer studied physics at ETH Zurich under notable professors including Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Scherrer. He began his PhD in 1955 on superconductivity, working with sensitive mechanical transducers after midnight to avoid vibrations. However, his doctorate was not completed until February 1960, when he was 27. His career-defining work—the scanning tunneling microscope—was invented in 1981 with Gerd Binnig at IBM Zurich, leading to the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics.

name: Inge de Bruijn
milestone_by_age_26: Won individual silver (100m butterfly) and bronze (50m freestyle) at the 1991 European LC Championships in Athens at age 17, plus relay gold and relay bronze at the same meet.
early_history_summary: De Bruijn tried several sports before specializing in swimming, starting from age seven. She debuted at the World Aquatics Championships in January 1991 at age 17, winning relay bronze, and then won multiple individual medals at the European Championships in August 1991. She made her Olympic debut at Barcelona 1992 but finished eighth in her events.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond being born in Barendrecht, Netherlands.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Dutch national swimming pipeline, early international competition, sprint specialization
evidence_summary: De Bruijn started swimming at age seven and tried multiple sports before specializing. By 17, she was competing at the World Championships (relay bronze, January 1991) and European Championships (individual silver and bronze, August 1991), representing the Netherlands at the highest level of international swimming. She was part of the Dutch national swimming pipeline, which provided access to elite coaching and competition. Her career stalled in the mid-1990s due to motivational issues, but she resurged in 1999 to win European Championship gold and was named European Swimmer of the Year before her triple-gold performance at the 2000 Sydney Olympics.
starting_point: Born in Barendrecht, Netherlands; family background not documented in reviewed sources beyond starting swimming at age seven.
current_position: Retired from competitive swimming; widely regarded as the most successful Dutch female athlete of all time with four Olympic golds and 11 world records; living in the Netherlands.

trajectory.event: Won individual silver (100m butterfly) and bronze (50m freestyle) at the European LC Championships in Athens, plus relay gold and bronze.
Made Olympic debut at Barcelona, finishing eighth in 50m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.
Won 50m freestyle gold at the European LC Championships in Istanbul and was named European Swimmer of the Year.
Won three individual Olympic gold medals (50m free, 100m free, 100m butterfly) at Sydney, setting world records in all three events.
Named World Female Swimmer of the Year for the second consecutive year after winning three golds at the World Championships.
Defended Olympic 50m freestyle title at Athens, becoming the oldest female Olympic champion in swimming history.

name: Peter Thiel
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Thiel co-founded the Stanford Review student newspaper at age 20 (1987) and completed his JD at Stanford Law in 1992, but his material career milestones—founding PayPal (1998), Palantir (2003), and investing in Facebook (2004)—all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Thiel was born in Frankfurt, Germany, and moved to the US as an infant. He studied philosophy at Stanford, co-founding the Stanford Review in 1987. He graduated in 1989, earned a JD from Stanford Law, and then worked as a securities lawyer and derivatives trader before founding Thiel Capital Management in 1996.
family_context_summary: Born in Frankfurt, West Germany; father was a chemical engineer. Family lived in Namibia and South Africa before settling in California in 1977.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemical engineer; no evidence of direct domain transfer to entrepreneurship or technology.
evidence_summary: Thiel attended Stanford University for his undergraduate and law degrees, co-founding the conservative Stanford Review newspaper in 1987 as a sophomore. While the Review built a network that later became the 'PayPal Mafia,' it was a student publication, not a material career milestone. After graduating law school in 1992, Thiel worked briefly as a securities lawyer and derivatives trader at Credit Suisse. His defining achievements—co-founding PayPal (1998, age 31), Palantir (2003), and being the first outside investor in Facebook (2004)—all occurred well after age 26.

name: Lorenzo Bandini
milestone_by_age_26: Made his Formula One debut in 1961 and won the Pescara 4 Hours world championship sports car race in a Ferrari 250 TRI/61 on August 15, 1961, at age 25, leading to a Ferrari contract for 1962.
early_history_summary: Born in Libya and raised in Florence, Bandini became an apprentice mechanic at 15 at the Freddi garage in Milan after his father died. His employer lent him cars to race in local events. He started racing cars in 1957 in a borrowed Fiat 1100, achieved a class win at the Mille Miglia in 1958, and became a star in Formula Junior in 1959-60, attracting Enzo Ferrari's attention.
family_context_summary: Born in Barce, Libya to an Italian family; father was murdered during the war when Bandini was young. Times were hard and at 15 he became an apprentice mechanic in Milan. He later married the garage owner's daughter.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family domain in racing; Bandini entered the sport through his employer Goliardo Freddi, a Milan garage owner who lent him cars and became his father-in-law.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Mechanic apprenticeship, borrowed cars, Formula Junior progression, Ferrari pipeline
evidence_summary: Bandini grew up in modest circumstances in Libya and Florence, losing his father during the war. At 15 he became an apprentice mechanic at the Freddi garage in Milan, where his employer recognized his talent and lent him cars to race. He started racing in 1957 (age 21) with a borrowed Fiat 1100, won his class at the Mille Miglia in 1958, and became a Formula Junior star in 1959-60. By 1961 (age 25), he made his F1 debut with Scuderia Centro Sud and won the Pescara 4 Hours in a Ferrari, earning a factory Ferrari contract for 1962. His mechanical background gave him deep domain proximity, and the Freddi garage served as an informal performance pipeline.
starting_point: Born in Barce, Libya to an Italian colonial family; father was abducted and murdered during WWII. Raised in Florence, left home at 15 to work as an apprentice mechanic in Milan.
current_position: Died May 10, 1967 at age 31 from injuries sustained in a crash at the 1967 Monaco Grand Prix; final role: Ferrari Formula One team leader.

trajectory.event: Achieved class victory at the Mille Miglia in a Lancia Appia Zagato, launching his racing career.
Made Formula One debut with Scuderia Centro Sud and won the Pescara 4 Hours in a Ferrari 250 TRI/61, earning a factory Ferrari contract.
Won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with Ludovico Scarfiotti in a Ferrari 250 P and finished runner-up at the 12 Hours of Sebring.
Won his sole Formula One race, the Austrian Grand Prix, and finished a career-best fourth in the World Drivers' Championship.
Won the Targa Florio endurance race for Ferrari.
Won the 24 Hours of Daytona with Chris Amon; fatally injured at the Monaco Grand Prix on May 7, dying three days later.

name: Yves Meyer
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Meyer was a PhD student at the University of Strasbourg at age 26 (1965); his doctorate was completed in 1966 at age 27. His major achievements—the Salem Prize (1970), Peccot Lectureship (1968), and Abel Prize (2017)—all came after age 26.
early_history_summary: Meyer grew up in Tunis and entered the elite École Normale Supérieure de la rue d'Ulm in Paris in 1957, coming first in the entrance examination. After military service (1960-1963), he began his PhD at Strasbourg in 1963, completing it in 1966.
family_context_summary: Born of French nationality in Paris in 1939; family exiled to Tunisia in 1944. Grew up in Tunis in a multicultural Mediterranean environment.
evidence_summary: Meyer was unusually gifted in mathematics, entering ENS-Ulm in 1957 by ranking first in the entrance exam. However, his doctoral studies at Strasbourg (1963-1966) were still ongoing at age 26. His first major recognition—the Peccot Lectureship—came in 1968-69, and the Salem Prize in 1970. His foundational work on wavelets and the Abel Prize came much later. While his ENS admission was exceptional, it represents an academic admission rather than a material career milestone by age 26.

name: Hagen Kleinert
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Kleinert completed his MS at Georgia Tech (1964) and was finishing his PhD at the University of Colorado (completed 1967) around age 26, but no notable research milestone or prize is documented by that age. His habilitation (1969) and major contributions came later.
early_history_summary: Kleinert was born in Festenberg (now Poland), grew up in Hannover, and studied physics at the Technical University of Hannover (1960-1963). He went to the US, earning an MS at Georgia Tech (1964) and a PhD at the University of Colorado, Boulder (1967) under Asim Barut.
family_context_summary: Born in Festenberg near Breslau (now Twardogóra, Poland); grew up in Hannover, Germany. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Kleinert studied physics at Hannover (1960-63) with distinction, then moved to the US where he earned an MS at Georgia Tech (1964) and a PhD at the University of Colorado (1967) under Asim Barut. He learned general relativity from George Gamow at Georgia Tech. His habilitation at Freie Universität Berlin came in 1969, and his major contributions—including the Duru-Kleinert transformation and variational perturbation theory—came in the 1970s and 1980s. No material research milestone is documented by age 26 beyond the completion of graduate degrees.

name: Zoran Živković
milestone_by_age_26: Won a gold medal at the 1967 Mediterranean Games in handball representing Yugoslavia at age 22, and helped Crvenka win the Yugoslav national championship in 1969 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Živković started playing handball at his hometown club Železničar Niš before moving to Crvenka, where he helped win the national championship in 1969. He later played for FAP and Metaloplastika before moving abroad to Germany. He competed for the Yugoslavia national team, culminating in Olympic gold in 1972.
family_context_summary: Born in Niš, DF Yugoslavia (now Serbia); family background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Yugoslav handball system, hometown club progression, national team selection
evidence_summary: Živković began playing handball at his hometown club Železničar Niš and progressed through the Yugoslav club system to Crvenka, where he won the national championship in 1969. He earned selection to the Yugoslavia national team, winning gold at the 1967 Mediterranean Games at age 22. The Yugoslav handball system was one of the strongest in the world during this era, providing an elite performance pipeline. Family background and early coaching details are not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Niš, DF Yugoslavia (now Serbia); family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired former handball player and coach; won Olympic gold as both player (1972) and coach (1984); last known coaching role was with Egypt's national team at the 2000 Olympics and 2001 World Championship.

Helped Crvenka win the Yugoslav national handball championship.

Coached Yugoslavia to Olympic gold at the Los Angeles Olympics as head coach.
Coached Yugoslavia to gold at the World Handball Championship.

name: Amanda Nunes
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold at the Pan American Jiu-Jitsu Championship in 2008 as a blue belt at age 20, and gold at the World Jiu-Jitsu Championship in 2009 as a purple belt at age 21, establishing herself as an elite grappler before transitioning fully to MMA.
early_history_summary: Nunes grew up in Pojuca, Bahia, Brazil, in a modest single-parent household. She started capoeira at age five and karate at seven. At 16, she began training Brazilian jiu-jitsu, and at 17 moved to Salvador to train at the Edson Carvalho academy, living at the gym. She won Pan American and World BJJ championships in 2008-2009 and made her pro MMA debut in March 2008 at age 19.
family_context_summary: Born in Pojuca, a small town outside Salvador, Bahia, Brazil. Parents split when she was four; raised by her mother, a school administrative assistant who sold hot dogs and sweets to support the family. Her mother trained boxing and her uncle was a Vale Tudo fighter.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother trained boxing and cornered Nunes's uncle in Vale Tudo fights, creating an early exposure to combat sports. Uncle was a Vale Tudo fighter.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Single-parent household, combat sports family exposure, gym immersion, Brazilian BJJ pipeline
evidence_summary: Nunes grew up in a modest single-parent household in Bahia, Brazil, with early exposure to combat sports through her mother (who boxed) and uncle (a Vale Tudo fighter). She started capoeira at five and karate at seven, then began BJJ at 16. At 17, she moved to Salvador to train full-time at the Edson Carvalho academy, living at the gym. She won Pan American BJJ gold (2008, blue belt) and World BJJ gold (2009, purple belt) before age 22, and made her pro MMA debut at 19. Her Strikeforce debut in January 2011 featured a 14-second KO. She joined the UFC in 2013 at age 25, though her first UFC title came in 2016 at age 28.
starting_point: Born in Pojuca, Bahia, Brazil to a single-parent household; mother was a school administrative assistant who sold hot dogs and sweets to support the family. Early exposure to combat sports through mother (boxing) and uncle (Vale Tudo).
current_position: Retired from UFC competition in 2023 after vacating the bantamweight title; widely regarded as the greatest female MMA fighter of all time; two-division UFC champion; living in Coral Springs, Florida.

trajectory.event: Won gold at the Pan American Jiu-Jitsu Championship as a blue belt and made her professional MMA debut.
Won gold at the World Jiu-Jitsu Championship as a purple belt.
Made Strikeforce debut with a spectacular 14-second knockout of Julia Budd.
Made UFC debut at UFC 163, winning via first-round TKO over Sheila Gaff.
Won the UFC Women's Bantamweight Championship by defeating Miesha Tate at UFC 200, becoming the first openly gay UFC champion.
Won the UFC Women's Featherweight Championship, becoming the first woman to hold two UFC titles simultaneously.
Retired from UFC competition after defending the bantamweight title against Irene Aldana, vacating the belt.

name: Vasily Ignatenko
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Ignatenko was a paramilitary firefighter who died at age 25 from radiation exposure sustained while responding to the Chernobyl disaster on April 26, 1986. His notoriety comes from the disaster itself and its dramatization, not from a personal career milestone or achievement by age 26.
early_history_summary: Ignatenko was born on a collective farm in the Brahin District of the Byelorussian SSR. He worked as an electrician before being conscripted into the Soviet Armed Forces in 1980, where he served as a military firefighter. After his service, he became a paramilitary firefighter with Fire Brigade No. 6 in Pripyat. He was a first responder to the Chernobyl disaster on April 26, 1986, and died 18 days later from acute radiation syndrome.
family_context_summary: Born on a collective farm in the Brahin District of the Byelorussian SSR; mother was a collective farm fieldworker and father was a tractor and truck driver. Third of five children in a working-class rural family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; family were collective farm workers with no connection to firefighting or public service.
evidence_summary: Ignatenko was a firefighter from a rural collective farm background in Belarus. He worked as an electrician, then served as a military firefighter during conscription (1980-1982), and became a paramilitary firefighter in Pripyat. On April 26, 1986, at age 25, he was among the first responders to the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, receiving a fatal dose of radiation. He died on May 13, 1986, in a Moscow hospital. His posthumous fame comes from the HBO series Chernobyl and Svetlana Alexievich's book Voices from Chernobyl, not from any personal career milestone or achievement by age 26.

name: Eliyahu Rips
milestone_by_age_26: Constructed a counterexample to the dimension subgroup conjecture while incarcerated in a Soviet psychiatric hospital around 1969-1971 (age 20-22), a significant result in group theory that attracted attention from the international mathematics community and contributed to his release.
early_history_summary: Rips was a math prodigy in Riga, Latvia, who entered the University of Latvia at age 15-16 and was the first high school student from Latvia to participate in the International Mathematical Olympiad. In April 1969, he attempted self-immolation in protest against the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, leading to two years of forced psychiatric internment. During this period, he debunked the dimension subgroup conjecture. He was released in 1971 after a petition from the mathematics community, moved to Israel in 1972, and completed his PhD at Hebrew University in 1975.
family_context_summary: Born in Riga, Latvian SSR to Jewish parents. Mother was from Riga and was the only one of nine siblings to survive the Holocaust; the others were killed at Rumbula. Father Aaron was a Jewish mathematician from Belarus whose first wife and children were killed during the Holocaust.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Aaron was a mathematician from Belarus, providing early mathematical exposure and domain fluency in a household shaped by Holocaust survival.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Math prodigy, father mathematician, Soviet repression, psychiatric hospital, IMO participation
evidence_summary: Rips was a mathematical prodigy who entered the University of Latvia at 15-16 and was the first Latvian high school student to participate in the IMO. His father was a mathematician, providing early domain exposure. In April 1969 at age 20, Rips attempted self-immolation protesting the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, leading to two years of forced psychiatric internment. During this incarceration, he constructed a counterexample to the dimension subgroup conjecture—a significant result in group theory. This achievement spread through the international mathematics community, leading to a petition for his release. He moved to Israel in 1972, completed his PhD at Hebrew University in 1975, and received the Erdős Prize in 1979. The adversity of Soviet repression and psychiatric imprisonment served as an extreme constraint that paradoxically concentrated his mathematical work.
starting_point: Born in Riga, Latvian SSR to Jewish Holocaust survivor parents; father was a mathematician from Belarus, mother was the only survivor of nine siblings. Grew up in Soviet Latvia with no exposure to Judaism.
current_position: Died July 19, 2024 at age 75 in Jerusalem; final role: Professor of Mathematics at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, known for the Rips construction, Rips machine, and Vietoris-Rips complex.

trajectory.event: Attempted self-immolation in Riga protesting the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia; subsequently incarcerated in a psychiatric hospital for two years.
Constructed a counterexample to the dimension subgroup conjecture during psychiatric internment; released after petition from the international mathematics community.
Completed PhD in mathematics at Hebrew University of Jerusalem on the dimensional subgroup problem, receiving the Aharon Katzir Prize.
Received the Erdős Prize from the Israel Mathematical Society for contributions to geometric group theory.
Was a sectional speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians and co-authored the controversial Bible code paper in Statistical Science.
Died on July 19, 2024 in Jerusalem after a career as a professor at Hebrew University.

name: C. N. R. Rao
milestone_by_age_26: Completed a PhD in chemical physics from Purdue University in 1958 at age 24 (in under three years), and joined the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bangalore as its youngest lecturer in 1959 at age 25.
early_history_summary: Rao was born in Bangalore to an academic family; his father was an Inspector of Schools and his mother tutored him at home. He completed his BSc at Mysore University at 17 and MSc from Banaras Hindu University at 19. He earned a PhD from Purdue University in 1958 at age 24 in under three years, then returned to India to join IISc Bangalore as its youngest lecturer in 1959.
family_context_summary: Born in Bangalore to a Kannada Deshastha Brahmin family. Father was an Inspector of Schools in the Mysore Education Department; mother was highly academic and tutored him at home in arithmetic and Hindu literature. Only child.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an Inspector of Schools, creating an academic home environment. Mother was skilled in arithmetic and teaching, providing early home tutoring. Parents made an academic environment that accelerated his education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Academic family, home tutoring, early university entry, Purdue PhD, IISc appointment
evidence_summary: Rao was born into an academic Brahmin family in Bangalore; his father was an Inspector of Schools and his mother tutored him at home. He was a precocious student, completing BSc at 17 and MSc at 19. He earned a PhD from Purdue University in under three years at age 24 (1958), then returned to India to join IISc Bangalore as its youngest lecturer at 25 (1959). His first research paper was published in 1954 while still a student. The combination of an academic family environment, elite institutional pipelines (Mysore University, BHU, Purdue, IISc), and early specialization in chemistry produced a rapid trajectory. He later became director of IISc (1984-94), founded JNCASR, and received the Bharat Ratna (2014).
starting_point: Born in Bangalore, Kingdom of Mysore, British India to a Kannada Deshastha Brahmin family; father was an Inspector of Schools, mother was an academically skilled homemaker who provided early home tutoring. Only child in an academic household.
current_position: Linus Pauling Research Professor and Honorary President of Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR), Bangalore; received Bharat Ratna (India's highest civilian award) in 2014; authored over 1,800 research papers and 58 books; age 91.

trajectory.event: Completed PhD in chemical physics from Purdue University in under three years, publishing his first research paper in 1954.
Joined the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bangalore as its youngest lecturer, beginning independent research in solid-state chemistry.
Moved to IIT Kanpur as Head of the Chemistry Department, building the department from scratch.
Received the Marlow Medal from the Royal Society of Chemistry.
Received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize, India's top science award.
Became Director of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), one of the most powerful scientific positions in India.
Founded the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR) in Bangalore.
Received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, becoming only the third scientist to receive it.

name: Robert C. Martin
